abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the leading causes of cancer death worldwide, with outcomes depending on the stages at diagnosis. Genomic and transcriptomic classifications are largely inferential because the genotype-phenotype relationship is non-linear and is influenced by post-translational regulation, protein turnover, and the tumor microenvironment (TME). Proteomics measures this functional layer directly. This review surveys proteomic technologies for CRC emphasizing mass spectrometry, affinity- and aptamer- based multiplex platforms, post-translational modification proteomics, spatial proteomics, AI-driven structural and predictive analysis, and multi-omics integration. Each platform is evaluated based on clinical questions, the supporting evidence and the barriers to implementation. Literature was drawn primarily from PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus (2020-2026), emphasizing advanced and translational applications. Alongside approved blood cfDNA and stool-RNA molecular tests, proteomics is a functional complementary technology that may improve biological interpretation, assay triage and treatment response prediction, although prospective clinical utility remains to be established. The decisive barriers are standardized biospecimens, validation evidence, clinical utility data and interoperable public data sharing. (169 words).

title: Identification and splicing assessment of a novel homozygous CFAP65 splice-site variant associated with oligozoospermia and complete asthenozoospermia.
abstract: Pathogenic variants in CFAP65 have been reported in male infertility with sperm motility defects. This study investigated a novel homozygous CFAP65 splice-site variant identified in a consanguineous family in which the proband presented with oligozoospermia and complete asthenozoospermia. Whole-exome sequencing was performed to identify candidate variants, followed by population- and disease-database annotation. Kinship and runs of homozygosity analyses were used to assess familial relatedness and autozygosity. RNA Splicer prediction and a minigene assay in HEK-293T cells were performed to evaluate the splicing effect of the identified variant. Semen analysis showed a sperm concentration of 8.1 × 10⁶/mL, with total and progressive motility of 0%. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous canonical splice-site variant in CFAP65 (NM_194302.4:c.645 + 1G > A), which was classified as pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines. ROH analysis showed increased autosomal homozygosity in the proband (FROH = 7.88%), supporting parental consanguinity. The minigene assay demonstrated complete exon 6 skipping, resulting in a 103-bp transcript deletion and a predicted frameshifted truncated protein p.(Pro182ArgfsTer29). This study expands the CFAP65 mutational spectrum and supports exon 6 skipping-mediated loss of function as the likely pathogenic mechanism. These findings highlight the value of genetic screening and functional splicing assessment in male infertility with sperm motility defects.

title: Recent advances in coarse-grained simulations of nucleic acid condensation.
abstract: Biomolecular condensates, formed through phase separation of multivalent biomolecules, play essential roles in cellular processes such as stress response, RNA processing, transcriptional control, and genome organization. Nucleic acids are increasingly recognized as important drivers and regulators of condensate formation and dynamics. This review examines recent advances in coarse-grained molecular simulations of dynamic nucleic acids and their phase transitions. We survey established computational frameworks validated against experimental data and discuss emerging applications that address increasingly complex systems. Existing studies reveal that base-mediated interactions emerge as dominant drivers in homotypic nucleic acid condensation and that simulation resolution fundamentally determines which physical phenomena are accessible and observable. We underscore that different modeling approaches at various resolutions provide complementary insights into nucleic acid condensation mechanisms and the driving forces. We emphasize the opportunities and challenges in extending these frameworks to capture the complexity of nucleic acid-mediated phase separation in biological contexts, while identifying important gaps in current modeling capabilities. Overall, molecular simulations at multiple scales have proven to be powerful tools for elucidating the mechanistic principles underlying nucleic acid condensates and their cellular functions.

title: Chemically stabilized long antisense oligonucleotides perturb RNA exosome function.
abstract: The interaction with intracellular proteins shapes the pharmacology and toxicity of RNA drugs like gapmers and siRNAs. Here, we identify the RNA exosome as a modification-sensitive interaction partner of long, chemically stabilized, single-stranded RNA drugs. Using proximity biotinylation proteomics, we observe preferential binding of the catalytic exosome subunits DIS3 and EXOSC10 to oligonucleotides stabilized by 2'-ribose modifications and phosphorothioate linkages. RNA drug binding correlates with exosome impairment as measured by dose-dependent stabilization of promoter upstream transcripts and accumulation of ribosomal RNA processing intermediates leading to reduced cell viability. Consistent with structural requirements for substrate threading through the exosome channel, oligonucleotides longer than 24 nucleotides can impair exosome function. Systematic variation of ribose and backbone chemistry reveals that exosome inhibition is highly sensitive to the spatial arrangement of chemical modifications and can be mitigated by incorporation of bulky 2'-MOE residues or alternative internucleoside linkages like mesyl phosphoramidate. In contrast to the clinically established RNA drug modalities, class-specific liabilities of emerging ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides remain poorly understood. Importantly, we demonstrate that ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides can be designed that preserve editing activity while minimizing exosome interference. These findings illuminate critical variables that must be considered in the safer design of next-generation RNA base editing therapeutics.

title: The m6A methyltransferase METTL3 in intervertebral disc degeneration: from molecular mechanisms to therapeutic potential.
abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IDD) is the fundamental pathological process underlying low back pain, a major cause leading to disability worldwide. As the most prevalent methylation modification in eukaryotic RNA molecules, N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is involved in various diseases and cellular processes by regulating RNA fate. Methyltransferase-like protein 3 (METTL3) is the sole catalytic component of the methyltransferase complex and mediates m6A deposition on target RNAs. METTL3 is ubiquitously expressed and modulated by a variety of factors at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels. METTL3 expression is significantly increased in degenerative nucleus pulposus tissue and shows a positive correlation with degeneration degree. Importantly, recent studies have demonstrated that METTL3-mediated m6A modification is able to promote the progression of IDD through multiple approaches, including extracellular matrix metabolism imbalance, inflammatory response, nucleus pulposus cell senescence and apoptosis, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Thus, METTL3 could represent a promising therapeutic target for IDD. This review systematically summarizes the latest advances regarding the role of METTL3 in IDD and underlying molecular mechanisms, and also highlights its potential translational implications.

title: At the crossroads of immunity and hijacking: dual roles of DDX proteins during host-virus interactions.
abstract: The DEAD-box (DDX) protein family, constituting a critical subgroup of the Superfamily 2 (SF2) helicase family, plays extensive roles in nucleic acid metabolism, gene expression regulation and innate immune signaling, and exerts a key regulatory role during viral infection. During viral infection, DDX proteins function as both RNA helicases and host restriction factors, exerting antiviral effects by recognizing viral nucleic acids, regulating signaling pathways and maintaining the host immune response. Conversely, through complex and diverse mechanisms, viruses can hijack or antagonize DDX proteins to facilitate their replication, transcription, translation and immune evasion. Focusing on the DDX protein family, this review systematically elucidates their molecular mechanisms of action across the life cycles of various viruses. Specifically, it examines the regulation of viral nucleic acid metabolism by DDX proteins, their influence on innate immune signaling pathways, and the molecular strategies employed by viruses to antagonize DDX proteins, while synthesizing the functional similarities and differences among members of the DDX protein family across distinct viral infections. This review aims to establish a theoretical framework for the in-depth analysis of virus-host interactions and the discovery of novel antiviral targets.

title: Mitochondrial Genome Characteristics of Rhodobryum laxelimbatum and Comparative Analysis of RNA Editing and Codon Usage Bias With the Chloroplast Genome.
abstract: Rhodobryum laxelimbatum is a traditional medicinal plant belonging to the genus Rhodobryum. To date, studies on this genus have focused primarily on its geographical distribution, chemical constituents, and biological activities, whereas genomic data within the genus are limited. The mitochondrial genome of R. laxelimbatum was sequenced, assembled, and annotated. Genomic structural features and simple sequence repeats (SSRs) were comprehensively characterized. Comparative analyses of RNA editing patterns and codon usage bias were performed using the mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes of R. laxelimbatum. The results revealed that the complete mitochondrial genome of R. laxelimbatum was 103,071 bp in length. It comprises 40 protein-coding genes (Nad7 is a pseudogene), 24 transfer RNA genes, and 3 ribosomal RNA genes. In total, 76 SSRs were detected. The mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes contained 189 and 608 RNA editing sites, respectively, with the conversion of hydrophilic amino acids to hydrophobic amino acids being dominant. Both organellar genomes exhibited the highest GC content at the first codon position. GC12 was significantly associated with GC3 only in chloroplasts with steeper regression trends. Mitochondrial genes exhibited greater variation in the effective number of codons (ENC), and most genes in both genomes clustered near the expected ENC curve. Parity Rule 2 plot revealed a distinct base-composition imbalance at synonymous third codon positions-mitochondria exhibited T3s > A3s with comparable G3s and C3s, whereas chloroplasts exhibited T3s > A3s and G3s > C3s. Five optimal codons were identified in the mitochondrial genome, predominantly ending in G/A/C, whereas nine were identified in the chloroplast genome, ending in A/U. Correspondence analysis demonstrated that codon usage bias was shaped by multiple interacting factors rather than a single determinant. This study provides crucial evidence for clarifying the evolutionary patterns of organelle genomes in Rhodobryum, and for understanding its genetic characteristics and molecular basis.

title: Generation of lachrymatory factor synthase-suppressed onion (Allium cepa L.) by Agrobacterium-mediated gene transfer for CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing.
abstract: Lachrymatory factor, an irritating volatile compound that induces tearing, is produced when onion bulbs are cut or chopped. Lachrymatory factor synthase (LFS)-specific suppression in onion may reduce the lachrymatory effect and enhance flavor and health-functional properties. Genome editing enables precise modification of target genes in plant genomes. However, no reports targeting genes controlling onion-specific traits have been published. Therefore, we aimed to generate onion plants with reduced LFS activity via clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) genome editing. Calli induced from primary roots were transformed with Agrobacterium tumefaciens carrying expression cassettes for CRISPR/Cas9, guide RNA, green fluorescent protein (GFP), and hygromycin resistance; callus lines with a high frequency of stable GFP expression were selected as "elite callus lines" suitable for transformation. Cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS), heteroduplex mobility assay (HMA), and Sanger sequencing confirmed mutations introduced into the LFS gene, and plants were regenerated from the confirmed LFS-edited callus lines. The LFS enzyme activity was lower in the leaves and bulbs of the LFS-edited plants than in those of control plants, while the LFS-edited plants exhibited severe growth abnormalities and failed to set seed, possibly due to long-term culturing to maintain the elite callus line. The present study demonstrates the feasibility of onion genome editing to modify a specific onion trait, namely, LFS activity. Our findings provide a basis for further development toward the ultimate goal of producing tear-free onions with enhanced health-functional properties.

title: Effect of disruption of PsPCP gene on fruit body color of Pleurotus salmoneostramineus.
abstract: The pink color of Pleurotus salmoneostramineus is due to a complex of pink color protein (PsPCP) and 2-dehydro-3-deoxylaetiporic acid A, which is a polyene pigment with the yellow color of Laetiporus sulphureus. In this study, we used the Cas9 ribonucleoprotein as a plasmid-free genome-editing tool to perform gene destruction in P. salmoneostramineus. Gene disruption via split-marker recombination by targeting the PsPCP gene using a pre-assembled Cas9/single-guide RNA system was introduced into the protoplasts of the wild-type monokaryotic P. salmoneostramineus strain N13 (A1B1) or N83 (A2B2). Disruptions at the target site were identified using genomic PCR, followed by sequencing. Strains N13 ∆PsPCP and N83 ∆PsPCP were matured on PDA agar plates and then cultivated on sawdust media to form the fruit body of the dikaryotic mutant N13 ∆PsPCP × N83 ∆PsPCP. In addition, compatible mutants of N13 ∆PsPCP × N83 and N13 × N83 ∆PsPCP were cultivated, and the pink coloring of these fruiting bodies was compared. N13 ∆PsPCP × N83 ∆PsPCP showed completely white fruiting bodies. In vitro color-developing reaction using 2-dehydro-3-deoxylaetiporic acid A extracted from the mutant with recombinant PsPCP, which showed no color, suggested that the amount of the compound was trace or degraded during fruit body formation.

title: RNA thermometers as temperature-dependent tools for enhanced recombinant protein production in precision fermentation.
abstract: Precision fermentation is a key technology for the future sustainable production of food proteins, bulk ingredients, and high-value recombinant products. However, process efficiency is often limited by the coupling of biomass formation and recombinant protein synthesis, leading to substantial carbon losses into non-recyclable biomass. Particularly for cost-sensitive bulk products such as food proteins, economically viable production requires highly efficient and dynamically controllable bioprocesses. RNA thermometers (RNATs) offer a promising inducer-free strategy for temperature-dependent control of recombinant protein production and dynamic bioprocess regulation, with the potential to improve carbon efficiency and product yields. In this study, a fluorescent reporter protein (EmGFP) under the control of a fourU (4U) RNA thermometer was evaluated in E. coli BL21 across a temperature range of 25-40 °C. Temperature-dependent regulation enabled maximal recombinant protein production at 35 °C, resulting in a 2.6-fold higher specific productivity compared to the derepressed control. The strongest RNAT-mediated regulatory effect was observed at 35.5 °C, highlighting the relevance of precise temperature control for recombinant protein production. Evaluation of altered carbon partitioning revealed a substantially increased carbon allocation toward product formation, while carbon partitioning into biomass and CO2 remained largely unchanged. Furthermore, the product-per-acetate yield increased more than threefold at induction temperature, indicating controllable carbon partitioning and reveals potential for decoupling approaches of biomass formation from recombinant protein production. This study demonstrates the successful implementation of an RNAT-controlled recombinant expression system enabling temperature-dependent regulation of protein production in E. coli. Quantitative analysis revealed controllable carbon partitioning toward recombinant protein synthesis and defined target temperatures for future process induction and switching. In contrast to conventional inducer-based systems, RNAT-mediated regulation enables dynamic control without chemical additives, supporting more resource-efficient bioprocess operation. However, fully exploiting RNAT-based process control will require advanced model-based strategies integrating temperature and feeding regimes, particularly for cost-sensitive precision fermentation processes such as food protein production. Overall, RNATs represent promising molecular control elements for future high-efficiency precision fermentation processes.

title: Restoring Neural Homeostasis via Class II HDAC Modulation: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Opportunities.
abstract: Class II histone deacetylases (HDACs) comprise class IIa enzymes HDAC4, HDAC5, HDAC7, and HDAC9 and class IIb enzymes HDAC6 and HDAC10, which differ substantially in structure, catalytic activity, subcellular localization, and neural function. Class IIa HDACs exhibit weak intrinsic deacetylase activity and function predominantly as signal-responsive scaffolds that couple calcium and kinase signaling to transcription through nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, recruitment of HDAC3-containing NCoR/SMRT corepressor complexes, and interactions with MEF2, CREB, and FOXO. Conversely, HDAC6 is a predominantly cytoplasmic deacetylase that regulates α-tubulin acetylation, cytoskeletal dynamics, axonal transport, autophagy, and proteostasis. Dysregulated class II HDAC signaling contributes to neurodegenerative diseases through convergent mechanisms involving synaptic dysfunction, maladaptive transcriptional repression, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and defective clearance of pathological proteins. Disease-associated substrates include amyloid-β and tau in Alzheimer's disease, α-synuclein in Parkinson's disease, mutant huntingtin in Huntington's disease, and TDP-43/SOD1 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Emerging evidence additionally links aberrant HDAC4/5 signaling to neurodevelopmental disorders through altered synaptic maturation, excitation-inhibition balance, and circuit development. This review integrates the structural and mechanistic biology of class II HDACs with their disease-specific roles and evaluates therapeutic approaches to restore neural homeostasis. Particular emphasis is placed on selective HDAC6 inhibitors, modulation of class IIa protein-protein interactions and subcellular trafficking, natural compounds, and RNA-based strategies. Finally, we discuss major translational challenges, including isoform specificity, brain penetration, context-dependent functions, and the need to distinguish catalytic from non-enzymic mechanisms when developing disease-modifying interventions for neurological disorders while preserving normal essential HDAC functions and minimizing off-target toxicity.

title: Uncovering essential RNA components of fusion oncoprotein condensates using bicon-seq.
abstract: Fusion oncoproteins drive aggressive leukemias by mediating aberrant gene expression within specialized biomolecular condensates that contain various biomolecules. While RNA is known to influence condensate properties, the RNA constituents of fusion protein-containing onco-condensates remain poorly defined. Here, we use bicon-seq (biotinylated-isoxazole-mediated precipitation of condensome and RNA sequencing) to globally profile condensate-associated RNAs from cellular samples. Using experimental perturbation of cytoplasmic RNA-containing condensates, we demonstrated that bicon-seq accurately quantifies changes in RNA solubility, that correlate with published RNA enrichment in these structures. In leukemia cells driven by the NUP98::KDM5A fusion oncoprotein, bicon-seq revealed highly conserved long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) that are associated with NUP98::KDM5A onco-condensates. Among them, the lncRNA Gas5 was highly expressed and essential for the proliferation of AML cells. Mechanistically, Gas5 co-localized with NUP98::KDM5A in condensates and modulated NUP98::KDM5A chromatin binding and the expression dynamics of differentiation/apoptosis-associated genes in AML cells. Together, our results introduce a novel approach to systematically profile condensate-associated RNAs and identify the lncRNA Gas5 as a critical regulator of NUP98::KDM5A-driven transcription in AML cells.

title: Psyllid glycine-rich antimicrobial peptides oligomerize to directly cleave zinc transporter ZnuA on the membranes of citrus Huanglongbing pathogen.
abstract: Huanglongbing (HLB), the most devastating citrus disease worldwide, is caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas) and transmitted by Asian citrus psyllid, Diaphorina citri. Currently, the potential role of the insect vector's innate immunity against CLas remains poorly understood. This study aimed to identify and characterize a 41-amino acid glycine-rich antimicrobial peptide from D. citri (DcGrAMP1), elucidate its molecular mechanism against CLas and related α-proteobacteria, and evaluate its efficacy in suppressing CLas in HLB-affected citrus under greenhouse and field conditions. Through genomic screening and CLas-induced expression validation, we obtained DcGrAMP1; combined with structural prediction, site-directed mutagenesis, molecular interaction techniques, and RNA interference, we elucidated its mechanism against CLas and regulatory pathway; through transgenic citrus construction and protein injection assays, we validated its CLas-suppressive efficacy under greenhouse and field conditions. DcGrAMP1 exhibits remarkable thermal stability. It oligomerizes through Arg26/Arg31 for bacterial membrane penetration, and Arg21 engages in binding-associated cleavage upon interacting with Asp153 of zinc transporter ZnuA on CLas membranes, thereby cleaving the adjacent peptide bond and triggering ZnuA degradation. CLas infection activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase-activator protein 1 (JNK-AP1) signaling pathway in the psyllid, thereby upregulating DcGrAMP1 expression. Overexpression or injection of DcGrAMP1 in citrus significantly reduced CLas titers and alleviated HLB symptoms. This work provides the evidence that insect AMPs can oligomerize to penetrate CLas membranes, and then directly cleave zinc transporter ZnuA on the membranes of citrus Huanglongbing pathogen.

title: RNA-Dependent RNA Polymerase (RdRp): Structure, Function, and Antiviral Targeting in RNA Viruses.
abstract: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) is the core catalytic enzyme that mediates RNA viral replication and transcription. The polymerase facilitates template and substrate channel assembly, nucleotide selectivity, and phosphodiester bond formation, making it an essential component of the viral life cycle. RdRps differ greatly in domain organization and replication initiation mechanisms across viruses, but their catalytic cores are highly conserved. The intrinsic low-fidelity replication of RdRp accelerates viral evolution, while some viruses fine-tune replication fidelity by proofreading exonucleases or accessory proteins that balance genome stability and adaptive variation. Given its conserved structure and non-redundant function, RdRp is a key target for broad-spectrum antiviral development, and numerous nucleoside (NIs) and non-nucleoside inhibitors (NNIs) are currently undergoing clinical or preclinical evaluation. However, three major obstacles limit inhibitor development: mutation-induced drug resistance, structural RdRp heterogeneity across viral species, and unfavorable pharmacokinetic properties. This review summarizes the structural basis and catalytic mechanisms of RdRp, discusses its functions during viral replication, genetic variation and virus-host interactions, and updates NI/NNI design, mechanisms, and development. We also dissect drug resistance mechanisms and inhibitor optimization strategies using advanced high-resolution structural and functional analyses. Overall, we provide insights for the rational development of broad-spectrum, potent antiviral agents with a low risk of RdRp resistance.

title: Small interfering RNA targeting protein Z-dependent protease inhibitor improves hemostasis in Von Willebrand factor- and Factor X-deficient mice.
abstract: Non-factor therapeutics have transformed the treatment paradigm in hemophilia A. Owing to their mode of action, these agents may also provide benefit for other rare bleeding disorders (RBDs) such as von Willebrand disease (VWD)-type 3 and Factor X (FX) deficiency. Targeting protein Z-dependent protease inhibitor (ZPI), a natural anticoagulant, is a novel strategy to enhance hemostasis. We evaluated the effects of ZPI post-transcriptional silencing using a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA (mTGM-148) in von Willebrand factor-deficient (VwfKO) mice and in mice with strongly reduced factor X levels (< 1%; f10low-mice). mTGM-148 reduced plasma ZPI antigen below 15% in both models. In VwfKO-mice, mTGM-148 significantly enhanced contact activation-initiated thrombin generation and normalized INTEM clotting parameters. In f10low-mice, thrombin generation was minimally affected, but EXTEM clotting parameters were significantly ameliorated. Importantly, mTGM-148 treatment significantly reduced blood loss in the tail clip model for both VwfKO-mice and f10low-mice. These data suggest that ZPI post-transcriptional silencing is a viable strategy to improve the hemostatic potential in both VWD-type 3 and FX deficiency. As such, ZPI inhibition represents a promising non-factor therapeutic approach for selected RBDs.

title: A c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) homolog from Macrobrachium rosenbergii participates in immune defense against Aeromonas hydrophila.
abstract: c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) is a key member of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) family, playing a vital role in the innate immune response of crustaceans by regulating the expression of antimicrobial peptide (AMP) genes. This research aimed to isolate and characterize a JNK gene from Macrobrachium rosenbergii designated as MrJNK. The full-length cDNA of MrJNK consisted of 1455 bp with an open reading frame (ORF) of 1266 bp encoding 421 amino acids containing a conserved serine/threonine protein kinase catalytic (S_TKc) domain. The phylogenetic tree of JNK proteins indicated that MrJNK and JNK from M. nipponense (MnJNK) were closely related, and were classified within the same clade as other JNK proteins from various crustacean species. The expression analysis by real-time RT-PCR showed that MrJNK was expressed in all examined tissues demonstrating the highest expression in the hemocyte. Following an immune challenge with Aeromonas hydrophila, the transcriptional levels of MrJNK were significantly upregulated in gill, hepatopancreas, hemocyte, muscle, and intestine. The functional role of MrJNK was investigated using RNA interference (RNAi) assay. Knockdown of MrJNK by dsRNA resulted to significant downregulation of anti-lipopolysaccharide factor 5 (ALF5), crustin (Crs), mannose-binding lectin (MBL), lysozyme (Lyz), and prophenoloxidase (proPO) transcripts. In addition, the cumulative mortality rate in MrJNK-silenced M. rosenbergii was significantly increased after A. hydrophila injection. Moreover, the expression levels of two antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and three immune-related genes were significantly inhibited after silencing MrJNK by dsRNA and A. hydrophila injection in prawns. These results indicate that MrJNK is required for normal transcription of these immune-related genes and is involved in the innate immune response of M. rosenbergii at the transcriptional level.

title: Affinity-optimized bispecific CAR-T cells targeting HLA-G and CD70 for the treatment of clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
abstract: Therapeutic options for clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) are limited. Recent clinical trials showed the efficacy of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy in treating ccRCC. However, heterogeneous expression of targeting antigen drives immune escape and impairs therapeutic efficacy. Bispecific CARs co-targeting two tumor-associated antigens may overcome this limitation. Human leucocyte antigen-G (HLA-G) and CD70 expression in normal and cancer tissues were analyzed using public RNA sequencing databases and immunohistochemistry of patient samples. An HLA-G CAR was engineered using its natural receptor human inhibitory receptors Ig-like transcript 4 (ILT4). The binding affinity of ILT4 to HLA-G was improved through structure-based rational design. A CD70 nanobody sequence was then incorporated into the HLA-G CAR to generate an HLA-G/CD70 bispecific CAR, together with a CD70-targeting short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to prevent CAR-T cell fratricide. A panel of linkers between the two antigen-binding domains was compared with optimize the CAR signal, and lead candidates were evaluated in vitro and in vivo using heterogeneous tumor models. HLA-G and CD70 were identified as ideal bispecific CAR-T targets to overcome the heterogeneity of ccRCC. An ILT4 mutant (Mut-5) with enhanced binding affinity to HLA-G was obtained. The HLA-G CAR derived from this high-affinity ILT4 mutant elicited enhanced antigen-specific cytotoxicity. An HLA-G/CD70 bispecific CAR was subsequently developed by connecting the affinity-optimized ILT4 mutant and a CD70 nanobody via an optimized (G4S)2 linker. To avoid fratricide of the bispecific CAR-T cells mediated by the expression of CD70, we incorporated a CD70 shRNA into the vector. The bispecific CAR showed specific cytotoxicity against both antigens, respectively, and mediated high antitumor activity toward double-positive tumor cells. Bispecific CAR-T cells effectively suppressed heterogeneous tumor growth in vivo and displayed less exhaustion compared with single-target CAR-T cells. We established an affinity-optimized HLA-G/CD70 bispecific CAR as a promising strategy to overcome antigen heterogeneity-mediated resistance and immune escape in ccRCC.

title: CRISPR-Scan: Cas13a Mismatch Tolerance Enabled Ultra-Multiplexed Detection of Same-Site Indels in Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
abstract: Detection of gene mutations related to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is crucial for its early diagnosis, personalized treatment, and recurrence monitoring. However, accurate detection of diverse mutations occurring at the same locus remains technically challenging. The CRISPR/Cas system, with its unique programmable nucleic acid recognition capabilities, provides a promising solution. Here, we elucidated that CRISPR/LwaCas13a is tolerant to consecutive substitutions but highly sensitive to insertions or deletions (indels) at specific positions of the spacer sequence, enabling rational CRISPR RNA (crRNA) design for multiplex detection of same-site indels. Guided by these principles, we achieved effective detection of ultra-multiplex nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1) c.863_864 4-bp insertions with a single crRNA, while maintaining specificity against the wild-type transcripts. We further established a one-pot CRISPR system, CRISPR-Scan, by integrating recombinase polymerase amplification with LwaCas13a cleavage. CRISPR-Scan enabled detection of mutations in backgrounds as low as 0.01%. In clinical validation, it identified NPM1 mutations in 43 of 120 AML patients, consistent with next-generation sequencing (NGS). Continuous monitoring of four AML patients indicated early recurrence with higher sensitivity than first-generation sequencing (FGS) and full concordance with NGS. A microfluidic chip and portable device further facilitate accurate AML mutation detection. This platform offers an efficient and convenient approach for early AML diagnosis and measurable residual disease (MRD) monitoring.

title: USP11 inhibits cuproptosis in non-small cell lung cancer by deubiquitinating IGF2BP2 to enhance the stability of m6A-modified ATOX1 mRNA.
abstract: Inducing cuproptosis is considered a novel strategy to impede non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) progression. ATOX1 suppressed cuproptosis by chelating free copper ions. This study seeks to elucidate the pathways that regulate ATOX1 upstream and thereby pinpoint molecular targets for activating cuproptosis in NSCLC. Cuproptosis was induced with ES-Cu. Malignant phenotypes were assessed using CCK-8, clonogenic, and Transwell assays. RNA immunoprecipitation, RNA pull-down, and actinomycin D chase were used to examine IGF2BP2-ATOX1 mRNA interaction and mRNA stability. Protein-protein interactions and ubiquitination were examined by co-immunoprecipitation. The co-localization of USP11 and IGF2BP2 was visualized by immunofluorescence. IGF2BP2 protein stability was assessed following cycloheximide treatment. Copper content was quantified using a commercial kit. Gene and protein levels were evaluated by RT-qPCR and Western blot. RNA-binding domain mutant rescue experiments were conducted to determine the functional requirement of IGF2BP2 KH domains. A subcutaneous xenograft model was established to validate the regulatory axis in vivo. ATOX1 suppressed cuproptosis to support NSCLC proliferation. IGF2BP2 bound to the CDS of ATOX1 mRNA via the m6A site at position 261, thereby enhancing ATOX1 mRNA stability. The KH3-4 domains of IGF2BP2 were indispensable for this regulation. Upregulation of ATOX1 by IGF2BP2 inhibited cuproptosis and consequently drove NSCLC proliferation. USP11 maintained IGF2BP2 protein stability via deubiquitination, leading to suppression of cuproptosis and promotion of NSCLC progression through the IGF2BP2/ATOX1 axis in vitro. In vivo, the USP11-IGF2BP2-ATOX1 axis might promote NSCLC tumor growth by suppressing cuproptosis. USP11‑dependent deubiquitination stabilized IGF2BP2, which subsequently increased ATOX1 mRNA stability in an m6A‑dependent manner. Elevated ATOX1 expression inhibited cuproptosis and thereby accelerated NSCLC progression.

title: Design foresight and model humility for omics inference.
abstract: Omics inference increasingly proceeds transcriptome-first: measure RNA, then ask how much biology can be extracted later. The ordering should be settled before the assay is chosen, not reconstructed from the data afterward. The first question is what the target requires to be directly observed; the second, what claims the data can honestly support. Design foresight means choosing assays, sampling, and orthogonal measurements based on the question and saying whether transcriptomics is primary, supporting, or insufficient for that claim. Model humility means refusing to promote computational output beyond what the data and assumptions can bear and writing measured, inferred, and predicted results in voices matched to their support. Using transcriptomics as the central case, we argue for question-first omics inference.

title: SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein hijacks host transcription by targeting eEF1A1.
abstract: SARS-CoV-2 variants display substantial genetic and phenotypic diversity, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying their effects on host gene regulation need further investigation. We performed a transcriptomic analysis of host responses to multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants, including Delta and Omicron. Despite their divergence, all variants induced a conserved transcriptional program in human lung epithelial cells characterized by activation of interferon regulatory factors (IRFs), immediate-early genes, and downstream cytokines. We identify the viral nucleocapsid (N) protein as a central driver of this transcriptional reprogramming, as N expression alone partially recapitulated the host response to infection. Mechanistically, N promotes recruitment of interferon regulatory factors and AP-1 transcription factors, RNA polymerase II, and the elongation factor eEF1A1 to promoters of pro-inflammatory genes, revealing a previously unrecognized nuclear role for eEF1A1. Disruption of the N-eEF1A1 interaction, genetically or pharmacologically using the eEF1A interactant plitidepsin, abolished transcriptional complex formation and reversed host gene dysregulation, identifying a conserved host-virus regulatory axis and potential pan-variant therapeutic target.

title: Short-term methionine starvation reshapes diurnal hepatic m6A RNA methylation.
abstract: Dietary methionine restriction improves metabolic health and has therapeutic potential in multiple disease contexts. Methionine metabolism regulates transmethylation reactions, including N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation, by modulating availability of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM). Both m6A methylation and methionine metabolism have separately been linked to circadian regulation, but whether dietary methionine influences circadian rhythms through m6A remains unknown. Here we show that short-term methionine deprivation induces diurnal variation in serum methionine and SAM and reprograms diurnal expression of m6A writers, erasers, and readers in mouse liver. Methylated RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (MeRIP-seq) at two timepoints (ZT9, ZT21) revealed that a methionine-deficient (MD) diet was associated with a roughly 10-fold increase in differentially methylated m6A peaks between timepoints relative to control, despite no change in methylation at core clock transcripts. These diet-induced oscillations arose at sites already methylated under the control diet, indicating that methionine restriction alters the rhythmicity of existing m6A marks rather than inducing new methylation, and were enriched in transcripts involved in RNA processing, translation, ubiquitination, and mTORC1 signaling. Integrating RNA-seq and proteomics, we found that a subset of these m6A changes co-occurred with altered mRNA and/or protein abundance, indicating gene-specific rather than global effects. Notably, reduced m6A methylation of Mat2a and Cbs, encoding enzymes central to methionine homeostasis, was associated with increased MAT2A and decreased CBS protein levels, respectively. These findings identify diet-induced, diurnally rhythmic m6A methylation as a candidate mechanism linking methionine metabolism to circadian biology and nominate specific m6A sites and pathways for future investigation.

title: STING engages PKR to drive lysosomal cell death in lung ischemia-reperfusion injury.
abstract: Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) has been implicated in multiple forms of cell death. However, the effector kinases that couple STING to these death programs remain poorly defined. Here, we show that during lung ischemia-reperfusion injury, mitochondrial DNA release engages the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-STING pathway to trigger lysosomal cell death (LCD) in mouse and rat models. In human lung epithelial cells, STING oligomerization at the endoplasmic reticulum drives autophosphorylation of double-stranded RNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR) at serine 33. This phosphorylation of PKR activates IκB kinase-NF-κB signaling independently of the canonical STING-TBK1 and PKR-eIF2α pathways. In turn, NF-κB induces LAMP3 transcription, promoting lysosomal membrane permeabilization and LCD. STING-PKR signaling is also observed in patient-derived lung epithelial cells and alveolar organoids. These findings identify PKR as a non-canonical STING effector and show that blockade of STING-PKR signaling attenuates epithelial LCD and lung injury.

title: Development of Versatile Nanoparticle System for Efficient Drug Delivery into Pulmonary Endothelium.
abstract: Drug delivery precisely to the pulmonary vasculature represents a formidable challenge. Pediatric Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (PARDS) is an urgent public health concern accounting for high mortality and long-term morbidity due to severe damage to lung endothelial cells (ECs). Advanced target-specific therapeutic interventions to protect lung vasculature in PARDS are in dire need. FOXF1 protein is a critical mediator of lung angiogenesis and vascular repair after injury. However, whether FOXF1 is a useful pharmacological target for PARDS is unknown. Herein, we developed a universal nanoparticle-based Lung Endothelial Drug Delivery (LEDD) system to deliver hydrophobic small-molecule compounds specifically to lung ECs but not to other cells or organs. Based on single-cell RNA sequencing, FOXF1 expression was decreased in lung ECs in the mouse PARDS model. We used LEDD nanoparticles to restore FOXF1 by delivering a novel FOXF1-activating compound, TanFe[F], which prevents FOXF1 protein degradation. LEDD-TanFe[F] treatment increased FOXF1 protein and its activity in lung ECs in vitro and in vivo. LEDD-TanFe[F] treatment was non-toxic, well-tolerated, and improved mice survival in the PARDS model. LEDD-TanFe[F] reduced endothelial permeability, improved vascular repair, and alveolarization in injured neonatal lungs. LEDD-supported drug delivery precisely to lung ECs is a promising therapeutic approach in PARDS.

title: Microglial Presenilin-1 modulates neuronal function and memory-associated behaviors.
abstract: Microglial cells, the macrophages of the brain parenchyma, are increasingly recognized to play a key role in synaptic plasticity and function. Presenilin 1 (PS1) is an essential protein involved in learning and memory; the loss of neuronal Presenilin function causes cognitive deficits and impaired synapse plasticity in mice. Here we show memory enhancement in male mice lacking PS1 in microglia (PS1ΔMG). Leveraging high-throughput RNA sequencing with single-cell deconvolution-analysis, we estimate that PS1ΔMG increases Cd52-lo microglial population, a proliferative group enriched in AP-1 responsive genes; and increases chemokines Ccl7 and Ccl8 In silico prediction of binding partners showed that microglial CCL7 may act via inhibition of neuronal CCR5, a receptor known to negatively regulate learning and memory. By profiling active neuronal populations via PhosphoTRAP the data showed a non-autonomous cell effect of microglial PS1 by modulating genes involved in neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity. Ex vivo electrophysiology and in vivo calcium imaging in freely behaving mice confirm these effects with functional changes in CA1 hippocampus as seen by increased NMDA/AMPA ratios and increased amplitude of neuronal Ca2+ transients in freely behaving animals, respectively. Remarkably, PS1ΔMG mice exhibited increased memory retention in contextual fear conditioning and novel object recognition. Together, these data suggest a novel mechanism where microglial PS1 negatively regulates neuronal activity through modulation of NMDAR and memory-associated behaviors.Significance Statement Microglia are increasingly recognized as active regulators of neuronal function, yet the molecular mechanisms that constrain their influence on synaptic activity remain incompletely defined. This study identifies microglial Presenilin-1 (PS1) as a key regulator of neuron-microglia signaling that shapes synaptic transmission and learning. We show that loss of microglial PS1 shifts microglia toward a transcriptional and signaling state that enhances NMDA receptor-dependent synaptic activity and improves memory, demonstrating that microglial molecular programs can directly modulate neuronal excitability. These findings establish microglial PS1 as a physiological brake on circuit plasticity and reveal that altering microglial signaling alone is sufficient to influence cognition. Targeting microglial regulatory pathways may therefore provide new strategies to enhance synaptic resilience and cognitive function in brain disorders.

title: CAP1 mediates chronic inflammatory pain-induced anxiety through cAMP/PKA/NF-κB signaling pathway in the anterior cingulate cortex of male mice.
abstract: A substantial subset of chronic pain patients suffers from comorbid anxiety, and this bidirectional exacerbation poses a major clinical challenge. Current pharmacotherapies have limited efficacy with notable side effects, underscoring the need for new targets. We successfully established a Complete Freund's Adjuvant (CFA) ‑induced chronic inflammatory pain model in male mice, which developed mechanical/thermal hyperalgesia, anxiety‑like behaviors, and Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC) synaptic plasticity abnormalities. RNA‑seq identified marked upregulation of ACC Adenylyl Cyclase‑Associated Protein 1 (CAP1). ACC CAP1 overexpression in naive mice selectively reduced mechanical pain and induced anxiety without affecting thermal nociception, whereas ACC CAP1 knockdown in CFA mice reversed anxiety and restored Excitatory/Inhibitory (E/I) balance while leaving pain thresholds unchanged. Mechanistically, CAP1 knockdown suppressed neuroinflammation via the Cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate (cAMP)/ Protein Kinase A (PKA)/Nuclear Factor kappa‑light‑chain‑enhancer of activated B cells (NF‑κB) pathway, as shown by reduced p‑PKA/p‑P65, cAMP, and pro‑inflammatory cytokines (Interleukin‑6, IL‑6; Interleukin‑1 beta, IL‑1β; Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha, TNF‑α). Consistent with this, an NF‑κB agonist completely blocked the anxiolytic effects of CAP1 knockdown, confirming that CAP1 acts through this signaling cascade to promote cytokine release and subsequent synaptic remodeling. Collectively, these findings establish ACC CAP1 as a critical mediator of chronic pain‑induced anxiety in male mice and suggest that targeting CAP1 may represent a promising strategy for precision intervention in pain-related affective disorders.

title: Suppression of plant immune responses enhances Agrobacterium-mediated transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana.
abstract: Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana is widely used for recombinant protein production and gene-function studies. However, agroinfiltration can activate host stress and defense responses, thereby limiting heterologous protein accumulation. To distinguish Agrobacterium-associated transcriptional responses from effects of the infiltration procedure, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) using an infection group (GV3101 carrying empty p1300), a buffer-only mock-infiltration group (Mock), and untreated wild-type (WT) plants. Relative to the mock group, the infection group contained 3,529 upregulated and 2,487 downregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with enrichment of defense- and stress-associated pathways, including "response to stress," "plant-pathogen interaction," and "plant MAPK signaling pathway". Tobacco rattle virus (TRV)-based virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) of selected candidates showed that silencing the ERF transcription factor PTI6 (pathogenesis-related genes transcriptional activator PTI6) increased GFP accumulation, and combined silencing of PTI5 and PTI6 produced a stronger effect than either single knockdown. Independent genetic testing using an eds1 CRISPR mutant further showed that loss of EDS1 (enhanced disease susceptibility 1) markedly enhanced transient expression of both GFP and GP3L-Flag, supporting a suppressive role of EDS1-associated immune signaling in agroinfiltration-mediated transient expression. In addition, stable NahG-Myc transgenic N. benthamiana lines derived from independent transformation events showed enhanced GFP accumulation, whereas HOS15 (high expression of osmotic stress-induced gene 15)-Flag lines did not improve transient expression under our conditions. Together, these results indicate that host immune responses can constrain transient expression and identify EDS1, PTI5/PTI6, and salicylic acid (SA)-related signaling as useful genetic targets for improving N. benthamiana as a transient expression chassis.

title: Loss of APOBEC1 disrupts RNA editing homeostasis and accelerates prion disease progression.
abstract: RNA editing is an epitranscriptomic mechanism that shapes transcriptome diversity and fine-tunes neuronal function. While adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing by ADAR enzymes has been extensively studied in neurodegenerative disorders, the role of cytidine-to-uridine (C-to-U) editing catalyzed by APOBEC1 remains largely unexplored. We investigated the impact of APOBEC1 on RNA editing homeostasis and prion disease progression using complementary in vitro and in vivo models. Global RNA editing and gene expression profiles were established in non-infected N2A and prion-infected sc-N2A murine neuroblastoma cells, under control conditions or following APOBEC1 depletion. APOBEC1 was silenced by shRNA-mediated knockdown to assess its regulatory contribution. In vivo disease progression was assessed in Apobec1 knockout mice subjected to RML prion infection to evaluate survival outcomes. Prion infection was associated with a global increase in RNA editing and an expanded repertoire of edited transcripts in sc-N2A cells. APOBEC1 depletion markedly reduced the overall editing levels, affecting both A-to-I and C-to-U editing events, reshaping editing patterns in transcripts associated with RNA and protein transport, cellular stress responses, synaptic signaling, and neuroimmune interactions. Consistently, Apobec1 KO mice exhibited accelerated body weight loss and significantly shortened survival following RML prion challenge. These findings support APOBEC1 as a contributor to RNA editing homeostasis and suggest that APOBEC1 loss reduces resilience to prion-induced neurodegenerative stress. APOBEC1 deficiency was associated with altered editome profiles in prion-infected cells and accelerated disease progression in the RML prion model.

title: Time-resolved transcriptomic analysis reveals envelope stress-mediated adaptation of Escherichia coli to the LPS transport inhibitor thanatin.
abstract: Gram-negative bacteria are a major cause of antibiotic-resistant infections due to their highly impermeable cell envelope which contains lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and prevents antibiotics from entering the cell. LPS biogenesis relies on the activity of the essential LPS transport machinery (Lpt), which represents an attractive and validated target for antibiotic development. The antimicrobial peptide thanatin impairs LPS transport by disrupting the assembly of the Lpt protein machinery, resulting in cell death. However, thanatin is not a suitable drug candidate due to its poor drug-like properties and the rapid emergence of resistance. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms underlying cell resistance and adaptation to thanatin is crucial for developing novel antimicrobial strategies. Here we performed RNA-seq-based kinetic transcriptomic analysis to investigate how bacterial cells respond to thanatin over time followed by a functional validation. We found that thanatin treatment induces a rapid activation of the Cpx envelope stress response system, followed by activation of Rcs phosphorelay and downregulation of the FlhDC regulon. Cpx regulated genes showed enrichment for pathways involved in cationic peptide resistance, stress regulation, protein folding, and peptidoglycan remodelling. Rcs upregulated genes were associated with capsule synthesis and biofilm formation. Finally, late response to thanatin suggests the involvement of phospholipid metabolism modulation and trafficking as a strategy to restore OM asymmetry. Overall, our results delineate the adaptive mechanisms employed by bacterial cells to counteract thanatin-induced stress through an interplay of multiple regulatory pathways controlling envelope integrity, stress responses, motility and biofilm formation.

title: Low Expression of PINK1 Suppresses Mitophagy in Sonic Hedgehog-Driven Medulloblastoma in Association With Activation of the PI3K/AKT Signaling Pathway.
abstract: Sonic Hedgehog-activated medulloblastomas (SHH-MBs) are aggressive, heterogeneous embryonal neuroepithelial tumors predominantly occurring in the pediatric posterior fossa. Postoperative recurrence and metastasis closely associate with aberrant mitochondrial subcellular localization and dysfunctional mitochondrial quality control. Mitophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of damaged or superfluous mitochondria, is intricately regulated by the PINK1-Parkin signaling pathway in metazoan cells. Nevertheless, the biological significance and the regulatory mechanisms underlying Sonic Hedgehog-mediated medulloblastoma (SHH-MB) proliferation, invasion, metastasis, and recurrence are not yet fully elucidated. In this study, integrated molecular and microscopy-based analyses revealed that PINK1 mRNA and protein levels were significantly downregulated in primary human SHH-MB specimens versus adjacent non-tumor brain tissues, as well as in a panel of SHH-MB cell lines. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) directly visualized impaired mitophagic flux, fragmented mitochondrial morphology, and accumulated damaged mitochondria in PINK1-deficient SHH-MB cells. In vitro functional assays showed that PINK1 overexpression minimally affected apoptosis but markedly suppressed cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, and potently restored mitophagic activity as validated by mitochondrial autophagy imaging. Combined RNA-sequencing, KEGG pathway enrichment, and Western blot verification further demonstrated that PINK1 depletion was associated with hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT signaling cascade. Collectively, our microscopy-supported mechanistic data demonstrate that PINK1 downregulation inhibits mitophagy in SHH-MB, an effect associated with sustained PI3K/AKT pathway activation. These findings highlight PINK1 as a promising diagnostic biomarker and potential therapeutic target for SHH-driven medulloblastoma, although the precise mechanistic relationship between PINK1 and PI3K/AKT signaling requires further investigation.

title: Cardiomyocyte-Specific LncRNA CSTPP Prolongs the Proliferation Window by Promoting CDKN1A Decay in Postinfarction Cardiac Regeneration.
abstract: Adult mammalian cardiomyocytes exhibit some capacity to reenter the cell cycle after ischemic injury. However, activated cardiomyocytes rapidly undergo cell cycle rearrest shortly after activation. Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as critical regulators of cardiac regeneration; however, their involvement in the process of cell cycle rearrest remains unexplored. Bulk RNA-sequencing was used to screen for lncRNAs differentially expressed during myocardial injury. Loss- and gain-of-function approaches were used to assess the role of lncRNA in cardiomyocyte proliferation and cardiac regeneration after myocardial infarction (MI). RNA pulldown and RNA immunoprecipitation were used to elucidate the underlying regulatory mechanisms. We identified a cardiomyocyte-specific lncRNA downregulated after myocardial injury and named it cardiomyocyte-specific transcript promoting proliferation (CSTPP). CSTPP overexpression enhanced neonatal rat ventricular myocyte proliferation, whereas its knockdown exerted the opposite effects. In vivo, CSTPP deletion attenuated cardiomyocyte proliferation, leading to exacerbated cardiac dysfunction post-MI. Conversely, CSTPP overexpression promoted cardiomyocyte proliferation and improved cardiac function. Furthermore, CDKN1A (cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1A) was found to be upregulated in cardiomyocytes localized at the border zone after MI, which was aggravated by CSTPP knockout and abrogated by CSTPP overexpression. Mechanistically, we showed that CSTPP interacts with YBX1 (Y box-binding protein 1), reinforcing the interaction between YBX1 and UPF1 (upstream frameshift 1), thereby enhancing UPF1 recruitment to CDKN1A mRNA and accelerating its decay. Notably, CSTPP was downregulated in heart samples from patients with MI. CSTPP overexpression decreased CDKN1A expression and facilitated proliferation in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes. Our findings identified CSTPP as a cardiomyocyte-specific lncRNA that functions to extend the activation window of the cardiomyocyte cell cycle after MI by stabilizing the YBX1-UPF1 interaction and thus facilitating the UPF1-mediated decay of CDKN1A mRNA. These results establish CSTPP as a promising therapeutic target for cardiac regeneration after MI.

title: Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses with experimental validation identify PLOD1 as a diagnostic biomarker and TGF-β1-responsive profibrotic mediator in dupuytren's disease.
abstract: Dupuytren's disease (DD) is a progressive fibroproliferative disease characterized by palmar fascia fibrosis, extracellular matrix deposition, and finger contractures. Reliable diagnostic biomarkers and regulatory mechanisms have not yet been fully defined. Firstly, integrate the public transcriptome datasets GSE59746 and GSE75152. Then, limma was used to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and combined with Weighted Gene Co expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) to screen candidate genes related to DD. PPI network analysis, functional enrichment, and four machine learning algorithms (LASSO, Boruta, Random Forest, and SVM-RFE) were applied to identify key biomarkers. Use CIBERSORT to assess immune infiltration. Analyze the single-cell RNA sequencing dataset GSE173252 to determine cell localization and pseudo time series analysis. Virtual knockout analysis is used to predict downstream regulatory targets. In vitro validation was conducted using TGF - β 1 stimulation and SB431542 inhibition. A total of 598 DEGs were identified, and the WGCNA brown module showed the strongest correlation with DD. Cross analysis identified 346 candidate genes, mainly enriched in extracellular matrix tissue, collagen containing matrix, and collagen trimer formation. Procollagen-lysine, 2-oxoglutarate 5-dioxygenase 1 (PLOD1) has been identified as the only overlapping biomarker among the four machine learning algorithms. PLOD1 is significantly upregulated in DD tissues and exhibits strong diagnostic performance, with an AUC of 0.908. Immunoassay showed a decrease in M0 macrophage infiltration, while there was a positive correlation between PLOD1 and M2 macrophages. Single cell analysis showed that PLOD1 was mainly enriched in chondrocyte related populations and increased along the late pseudotime trajectory. Virtual knockout indicates that FGF7 is a key downstream gene. TGF - β 1 significantly induces PLOD1 and pro fibrotic markers, while SB431542 inhibits these effects. PLOD1 is a promising biomarker and potential functional regulator for DD diagnosis, closely related to extracellular matrix remodeling, pro fibrotic signaling, and immune microenvironment changes.

title: Aberrant splicing caused by a homozygous AK2 c.498 + 1G > A variant in a patient with reticular dysgenesis and concurrent B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
abstract: Reticular dysgenesis (RD) is a rare autosomal recessive severe combined immunodeficiency characterized by profound neutropenia, T-cell lymphopenia and sensorineural hearing loss, and is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in AK2. We identified a homozygous AK2 splice-site variant (c.498 + 1G > A) in a boy with RD and concurrent B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), a clinical combination not previously reported in association with an AK2 variant. An in vitro minigene assay showed that c.498 + 1G > A disrupts the canonical 5' splice donor site and generates an aberrant transcript carrying a 4-bp intronic insertion after exon 5, which causes a frameshift and introduces a premature termination codon; the transcript is predicted to be degraded by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay or, if translated, to yield a non-functional truncated protein, leading to loss of AK2 function. The variant was classified as pathogenic according to the ACMG/AMP criteria. As patient-derived material was unavailable, we re-analyzed publicly available RNA-seq data from AK2-knockout human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (GSE179320) and identified six hub genes (APOE, TREM2, CD68, CD36, IRF8 and CD163), which we further validated at the mRNA level in AK2-knockdown HL-60 cells, with IRF8 showing the most pronounced upregulation. This study characterizes the splicing defect caused by this variant and identifies candidate AK2-associated genes; the coexistence of RD and B-ALL is reported as a clinical observation requiring further investigation.

title: Treatment-refractory autoimmune glial fibrillary acidic protein astrocytopathy: Clinical features, predictive models, therapy.
abstract: A subset of glial fibrillary acidic protein astrocytopathy experiences treatment-refractory disease course, yet the clinical and immunological features defining this subgroup remain incompletely characterized. Patients were classified as treatment-refractory (n = 23) or treatment-responsive (n = 30). Clinical, imaging, and outcomes were compared. For subgroup analyses, refractory patients were divided into three groups: no immunoadsorption/plasma exchange (IA/PE) (n = 9), IA/PE monotherapy (n = 4), and IA/PE plus rituximab (n = 10), with functional outcomes compared across groups. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) from refractory patients was applied to a passive transfer mouse model, and single-cell RNA sequencing was performed to explore underlying pathogenic mechanisms. The treatment-refractory group had higher proportion of the meningoencephalomyelitis phenotype (82.6% vs. 53.3%, P = 0.026) and more frequent disturbances of consciousness (65.2% vs. 30.0%, P = 0.011), paraplegia (78.3% vs. 33.3%, P = 0.001), and peripheral nervous system involvement (89.5% vs. 22.2%, P < 0.001). Refractory patients had elevated cerebrospinal fluid glial fibrillary acidic protein and neurofilament light chain levels. Refractory patients more frequently exhibited spinal cord lesions involving three or more segments (65.2% vs. 21.4%, P = 0.002). Disability at last follow-up was greater in the refractory group (median modified Rankin Scale score 3 vs. 1, P < 0.0001). Firth penalized regression model identified peripheral nervous system involvement as the independent predictor of treatment refractoriness (odds ratio = 10.74, P = 0.006). Among refractory patients, the IA/PE-plus-rituximab group had significantly lower long-term mRS scores than the no-IA/PE group (adjusted P = 0.031). GFAPA-IgG from refractory patients induced CD45+ cell infiltration in mouse brain. Single cell analysis demonstrated activation of complement and inflammatory pathways, with astrocytes adopting a pro inflammatory state. Treatment refractory disease is marked by severe central and peripheral nervous system injury. Convergent clinical and experimental evidence provides a rationale for B cell targeted therapies.

title: The role of rapamycin in neural tube defects: insights from bioinformatics analysis and experimental validation.
abstract: Neural tube defects (NTDs) are the most severe congenital malformations of the central nervous system. Fetal developmental homeostasis disruptions heighten NTDs risk through aberrant maternal-fetal signaling and periconceptional medication exposure. Rapamycin, an inhibitor of the mTOR signaling pathway, is a widely used clinical drug whose effects on embryonic neural development remain unclear. This study aimed to identify the potential drug targets for rapamycin in embryonic neural development. 18 rapamycin-NTDs targets were obtained by the network pharmacology approach. Functional enrichment analyses discovered they were associated with cell migration. AVPR2, CYP2C19, EPHB4, MMP9 and OXTR were identified as pivotal regulators mediating the effects of rapamycin on NTDs through machine learning. Immune infiltration analysis revealed the proportion of follicular helper T cells in the NTDs group was significantly lower and the pivotal genes were closely related with immune cell populations. Through single-cell RNA sequencing analysis, we identified 7 major cell types and confirmed the expression of rapamycin-NTDs key genes across them. Rapamycin-induced NTDs murine model displayed the NTDs incidence was 21.5% following 0.5mg/kg rapamycin exposure. Subsequent animal and cell experiments confirmed that MMP9 exhibited the strongest correlation in rapamycin-induced NTDs, which could regulate cell migration. Our results suggested that rapamycin may impair cell migration by suppressing MMP9, thereby contributing to the development of NTDs. These findings provide an experimental basis for elucidating the potential mechanisms of rapamycin in embryonic neural development. MMP9 might represent a target strategy for prevention and a potential biomarker for the early diagnosis of mTOR pathway abnormality or rapamycin-induced NTDs.

title: ATF6-mediated GTPase RHOQ promotes liver cancer progression via enhancing aerobic glycolysis through PAK1 phosphorylation.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) ranks among the most prevalent malignant tumours worldwide, accounting for approximately 90% of primary liver cancer cases, with the highest incidence observed in Asia. Activating Transcription Factor 6 (ATF6) is an endoplasmic reticulum stress-responsive transcription factor. Our previous studies have demonstrated that ATF6 contributes to HCC tumourigenesis and progression through signalling pathways such as ATF6-CTH-Keap1-mTORC1 and ATF6-PPM1H-RPS6KB1. RNA sequencing identified ATF6 transcriptional targets, with Ras homolog family member Q (RHOQ) validation via chromatin immunoprecipitation and electrophoretic mobility shift assay. RHOQ expression and clinical significance were analysed in HCC cohorts. Functional assays assessed proliferation, migration, invasion and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Tumour growth was evaluated in orthotopic (NOG mice) and subcutaneous (nude mice) models. Mechanistic analyses were performed to characterise RHOQ-mediated regulation of p21-activated kinase 1 (PAK1) signalling and metabolic remodelling. Furthermore, therapeutic synergy between PAK1 inhibitor IPA-3 and Glypican-3 (GPC3)-CAR T cells was tested. We identified RHOQ as a direct transcriptional target of ATF6. Clinically, elevated RHOQ expression correlated with poorer progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with HCC. Functionally, RHOQ promoted the proliferation and metastasis of liver tumour cells. Correspondingly, RHOQ knockdown markedly suppressed tumour growth in xenograft models, with consistent results observed in a hydrodynamic tail vein injection(HTVi) model. Mechanistic investigations revealed that RHOQ directly bound to PAK1, promoted its phosphorylation and activation and thereby drove aerobic glycolysis in liver tumour cells. Furthermore, combined treatment with the PAK1-specific inhibitor IPA-3 and GPC3-targeted CAR T-cell therapy produced a significant synergistic anti-tumour effect. In summary, this study systematically delineated the importance of the ATF6-RHOQ-PAK1 signalling cascade in driving liver cancer progression and provided a rationale for the design of targeted combination therapies. RHOQ is a novel direct transcriptional target of ATF6 in HCC. High RHOQ expression is associated with unfavourable clinicopathological features and poorer PFS. RHOQ drives HCC progression via PAK1 activation and aerobic glycolysis. Combining the PAK1-specific inhibitor IPA-3 with GPC3-targeted CAR T-cell therapy produces a potent synergistic anti-tumour effect.

title: Combined elevated C-reactive protein and detectable plasma RNA has predictive value for hospitalization during an outpatient COVID-19 convalescent plasma clinical trial.
abstract: Laboratory biomarkers that predict progression from mild COVID-19 to hospitalization are not well defined. To evaluate the performance of C-reactive protein (CRP) and plasma SARS-CoV-2 RNA for predicting hospitalization among mild COVID-19 outpatients enrolled in a randomized controlled trial of COVID-19 convalescent plasma (CCP). CRP and plasma SARS-CoV-2 RNA were measured in 487 outpatient trial participants screened before March 2021. Weighted analyses accounting for sampling probabilities were used to estimate positive predictive values (PPVs) and sensitivities for progression to hospitalization, with performance compared across trial arms. Elevated CRP (>1 mg/dL) was present in 27% (131/487) of participants, and plasma SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detectable in 15% (74/487). In weighted analyses, PPVs for hospitalization were 15% (95% CI, 10-21) for elevated CRP alone, 25% (95% CI, 16-35) for detectable plasma RNA alone, and 37% (95% CI, 23-52) when both biomarkers were present. Among participants with elevated CRP and plasma RNA >500 copies/mL, PPV increased to 72% (95% CI, 37-100). Elevated CRP demonstrated 100% sensitivity for hospitalization in CCP-transfused participants and 54% in control plasma-transfused participants, while detectable plasma RNA demonstrated sensitivities of 60% and 50%, respectively. Among individuals meeting severe COVID-19 risk criteria based on sex, age, obesity, or comorbidities, the combination of normal CRP and undetectable plasma RNA have a high negative predictive value for hospital progression risk. The combination of elevated CRP and detectable plasma SARS-CoV-2 RNA improves laboratory-based risk stratification for progression to hospitalization among outpatients with mild COVID-19.

title: Cross-sectional study on norovirus genotyping and epidemiology among hospitalised children with acute gastroenteritis in Tianjin, North China, 2020-2023.
abstract: To understand the molecular epidemiological and clinical characteristics of norovirus in children with acute gastroenteritis in Tianjin from 2020 to 2023. A total of 6714 faecal samples were collected from children aged 0–17 years with acute gastroenteritis who visited Tianjin Children’s Hospital from August 2020 to July 2023. All samples were initially screened for norovirus using reverse transcription PCR. The polymerase region and capsid protein region of the initially screened positive samples were amplified using reverse transcription PCR, the sequences were aligned and a phylogenetic tree was constructed. Of the 6714 children with acute gastroenteritis, 1395 (20.78%) tested positive for norovirus in stool samples. Among them, 810 were male (20.62%, 810/3929) and 585 were female (21.01%, 585/2785). Norovirus detection rate showed seasonal differences, with the detection rates of norovirus-RNA in spring, summer, autumn and winter being 27.97% (605/2163), 11.04% (195/1767), 12.04% (141/1171) and 28.15% (454/1613), respectively. 155 norovirus-positive specimens were subjected to dual-region typing and clinical symptom-related information was collected. They were divided into nine genotypes, all of which were GII type. The three most prevalent genotypes were GII.4(P16), GII.3(P12) and GII.2(P16). The GII.4(P16) genotype accounted for 38.06% (59/155), the GII.3(P12) genotype for 27.74% (43/155) and the GII.2(P16) genotype for 19.35% (30/155). From 2020 to 2023, the main age of onset of diarrhoea in children in Tianjin was 13–36 months, with a higher incidence in spring and winter. The most susceptible genotypes were GII.4(P16), GII.3(P12) and GII.2(P16). Abdominalgia, aminotransferase, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin and neutrophil count are statistically associated with norovirus genotypes in paediatric patients. Close monitoring of the norovirus’s spread in the population is crucial to prevent outbreaks in childcare facilities, schools and other places where children congregate, which could increase the risk of severe cases, burden family care and strain public health control efforts.

title: Prior Venous Thromboembolism Defines Distinct Genetic and Molecular Phenotypes in Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension.
abstract: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) has traditionally been considered a long-term complication of pulmonary embolism. However, a substantial proportion of patients have no history of venous thromboembolism (VTE), suggesting underlying biological heterogeneity. We analyzed clinical and imaging characteristics of 712 patients with CTEPH stratified by prior VTE history. Whole-genome sequencing was performed in all patients and 2952 healthy controls to assess common variants. Bulk RNA sequencing of pulmonary endarterectomy tissues and plasma protein quantification were integrated to identify and validate subgroup-specific molecular signatures, with further validation in tissue and primary endothelial cells. Patients with CTEPH and prior VTE (n=576, 80.9%) exhibited a distinct thrombotic phenotype with more proximal disease distribution (92.5% versus 66.2%) and greater likelihood of undergoing pulmonary endarterectomy (22.6% versus 3.7%). Genome-wide association study in CTEPH-VTE(+) patients versus controls identified coagulation-related loci at ABO (rs676996, P=1.1×10-9) and FGG (rs7681423, P=2.5×10-8), with high genetic correlation with pulmonary embolism (rg=0.52, P=0.028). In contrast, no consistent genomic signal was identified in patients without prior VTE. Integrative multiomics (transcriptome-wide association study, MAGMA, and bulk RNA sequencing differential expression analysis) convergently prioritized CTSS (cathepsin S) as a key molecular candidate in CTEPH-VTE(+). CTSS was consistently elevated in plasma, pulmonary endarterectomy tissue, and primary endothelial cells from CTEPH-VTE(+) patients and promoted endothelial proliferation via ERK signaling, which was attenuated by the selective CTSS inhibitor LY3000328. Stratification by prior VTE history reveals biologically distinct CTEPH phenotypes with divergent genetic architectures and identifies cathepsin S as a genetically nominated therapeutic target for thrombosis-associated pulmonary vascular remodeling.

title: Pan-cancer multi-omics analysis reveals upregulation of the POLE2 subunit of DNA polymerase epsilon and its associations with patient survival and cellular pathways beyond DNA replication.
abstract: DNA polymerase epsilon (Polε) is essential for high-fidelity leading-strand synthesis. It comprises a catalytic subunit, POLE, and three accessory subunits, including POLE2. In contrast to POLE, the biological functions and clinical significance of POLE2 remain unexplored. POLE2 is vital for the assembly of Polε and for interactions with the CMG helicase. Yeast studies show that dysfunction of its ortholog, Dpb2, causes genomic instability and impaired cell cycle progression. To investigate the significance of POLE2, this study provides a comprehensive multi-omics analysis across tumor types. We show that POLE2 upregulation is associated with decreased overall survival in a cancer-type-specific manner. Its expression levels, rather than copy number variation (CNV), emerge as a more reliable prognostic marker. POLE2 expression regulatory mechanisms include promoter methylation, isoform usage, and epigenetic regulators. Elevated POLE2 messenger RNA levels rarely translate into increased protein levels, possibly because of abundant non-coding isoforms. Co-expression and pathway enrichment analyses reveal an association between POLE2 and transcriptional regulation involving E2F, EZH2, and RB. Our findings highlight POLE2 as a contributor to genome stability, a candidate cancer biomarker, and a possible therapeutic target.

title: Pathological mechanisms of long non-coding RNA FOXD2-AS1 promoting osteosarcoma mediated by the COI-1/OCN/Runx-2 signaling pathway.
abstract: Osteosarcoma (OS) is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents. Despite three decades of research efforts, no significant improvement in patient survival rates has been achieved, highlighting the urgent need for in-depth investigation into its pathogenesis to develop novel therapeutic strategies and more effective drugs. FOXD2-AS1, a long non-coding RNA, has been implicated in the prognosis and survival of various cancers, but its role in OS remains underexplored. This study therefore aimed to investigate the functional involvement of FOXD2-AS1 in OS progression and to evaluate a biocompatible delivery system for its in vitro and in vivo application. We synthesized mPEG-PDPA hydrogel via free radical polymerization of 2-(diisopropylamino)ethyl methacrylate (PDA) and polyethylene glycol monomethyl ether acrylate (mPEG-AC), and employed this hydrogel as a delivery vehicle for FOXD2-AS1. The biocompatibility and safety of the empty hydrogel were first validated through both in vitro cell assays and in vivo animal experiments. To explore the mechanistic actions of FOXD2-AS1, we performed real-time quantitative PCR and Western blot analyses, and conducted transcriptome profiling to identify downstream pathways and associated genes. Our results demonstrated that the mPEG-PDPA hydrogel itself was non-toxic and reliable as a delivery vehicle. Functionally, FOXD2-AS1 promoted alkaline phosphatase (ALP) release and exacerbated the inflammatory response, thereby accelerating the development and deterioration of OS. Mechanistically, FOXD2-AS1 activated the F-box protein Coronatine Insensitive 1 homolog (COI-1)/OCN/Runx-2 signaling pathway, as confirmed by qPCR and Western blot. Transcriptome analysis further revealed that this process involved changes in cell migration, apoptosis, and cell cycle regulation, with CPS1-IT1, ANKRD10-IT1, TBC1D3P1-DHX40P1, and RGS5 identified as key associated genes. Collectively, our findings provide new insights into the pathological mechanisms of OS and offer valuable data support for future therapeutic strategy development.

title: Nox4 Mediates Diastolic Function in a Genetic Model of Pitx2 Haploinsufficiency.
abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) commonly coexists with atrial fibrillation (AF), but shared mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we hypothesized that Pitx2, a transcription factor located near the strongest genetic locus associated with AF in humans, increases susceptibility to HFpEF-like remodeling. We also sought to understand pathways that might be central to this increased risk. Male and female Pitx2+/- mice and wild-type littermates received 3-week subcutaneous osmotic pump infusion of saline or angiotensin II (Ang II; 500 ng/kg/min). Cardiac structure and function were assessed by echocardiography and catheterization, and functional capacity by exercise treadmill. RNA transcriptomic profiling was performed to identify candidate pathways. In a separate cohort, Ang II-treated mice were randomized to oral GKT136901 (30 mg/kg/day) or vehicle during infusion. After Ang II infusion, Pitx2+/- mice developed exaggerated HFpEF-like changes, including greater left ventricular hypertrophy, left atrial enlargement, diastolic dysfunction, elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, and reduced treadmill performance. RNA-seq showed enrichment of metabolic and stress-response pathways with selective upregulation of Nox4, confirmed by RT-qPCR.
